How a Payment System Learns Who Gets Paid

By oht_editor
on October 06, 2026

FacebookTwitterEmailCopy LinkMessengerPrintShare

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:58
Instaread

Checking the xrp price today tells you one number. Using XRP in a payment application requires something else entirely. A price screen only needs to identify an asset. A payment system needs more.

It must know who should receive the funds, which customer they belong to, and which record to update once the money arrives. The main issue is how a payment system distinguishes one payment from another when many payments arrive at the same address.

The Need for More Than an Address

A blockchain address can tell the network where value should go. It can’t always tell the business what the payment is for. Anyone who has sent a bank transfer knows this problem.

A routing number sends funds to the right bank. An account number or reference line tells the bank which customer to credit. Payment services on blockchain networks face a similar issue.

A company handling transfers for many customers doesn’t need a separate address for each one. It can use a shared address if it can sort payments once they land in a shared account.

How DestinationTag Adds Context

The XRP Ledger includes an optional field called DestinationTag in its payment transaction type. It’s a number attached to a transfer. Hosted services can use it to identify which customer or purpose a payment relates to.

Consider a business processing crypto transfers for hundreds of accounts through one XRPL address. Without the expected identifying information, the ledger transaction alone may not tell the receiving service which internal customer or merchant account should receive credit. A destination tag gives the receiving application a way to sort them out.

What DestinationTag Does Not Do

It helps to be precise here, since the terminology can be confusing. A destination tag isn’t a second wallet, a separate cryptocurrency, or a transaction of its own. Instead, it’s optional identifying information attached to a payment transaction.

XRP is the XRP Ledger’s native asset. The DestinationTag field provides additional context that a receiving service can use to connect an incoming payment to the appropriate customer or account. The two serve different purposes. XRP represents the value being transferred, while the destination tag can help explain how the receiving application should handle that transfer.

A Hypothetical Look at Shared Destinations

Consider a payment processor serving businesses in Thousand Oaks or nearby Agoura Hills. The processor could use one shared XRPL address to receive payments for multiple merchant accounts. The address tells the network where the payment should go, whereas a destination tag gives the receiving service information it can use to match that payment to the appropriate account.

If a customer omits a required tag, the payment may still reach the shared address but arrive without enough information for the processor to determine which account should receive credit. This is a data-matching problem, not a security failure.

How InvoiceID Identifies a Payment’s Purpose

XRPL also supports a separate optional field called InvoiceID. It’s a 256-bit identifier that can represent an invoice or another specific payment reason. It exists alongside the DestinationTag, but does not replace it.

The two fields solve related but different problems. DestinationTag typically identifies a recipient or account within a shared address. InvoiceID can identify the reason for a payment, such as a specific invoice it is meant to settle.

A validated transaction also carries a unique hash, separate from either field. The hash identifies the transaction itself. Tags and invoice identifiers help a business connect that transaction to its own books.

From Ledger Entry to Business Record

Once you strip away the technical jargon, you realize that adding identifying details to a payment is a common business practice. Utility bills carry account numbers. Paper checks carry memo lines. Wire transfers often require a reference code, so the receiving bank applies funds correctly. Blockchain payment systems face the same basic need for structured information. 

Thomas Gregory, Binance’s vice president of payments and fiat, described the company’s approach in a May 2026 Binance Pay announcement reported by FinanceFeeds: “For much of its history, crypto has been seen primarily as something to trade or hold, rather than use in everyday life,” he said. “Rather than asking for merchants and users to adopt a new system, our focus is on making crypto usable within existing local payment environments.”

Structured identifiers let software do the sorting instead of a person checking every incoming payment by hand. Once the receiving service matches a payment to the correct customer or account, the information can trigger the next step in the business process. The system might update an account balance, mark an invoice as paid, or confirm an order is complete. 

For anyone in the Conejo Valley, the takeaway isn’t about XRP’s value on any given day. Instead, it’s that useful payment technology often works in the background. It gives a business the information it needs to connect a transaction to the right customer and update the appropriate record.
